item.title: Prediction Markets, Part 1: How a Price Becomes a Forecast
item.description: Part 1 of a two-parter built from a knowledge graph on prediction markets. A contract pays one dollar if an event happens, so its price reads as a probability. We cover why economists think that should work (Hayek's idea that prices pool scattered knowledge, plus Arrow-Debreu and efficient markets), the automated market maker that keeps thin markets trading, corporate markets at firms like Google, and how the law shaped the field: Iowa Electronic Markets, Intrade's shutdown, Polymarket's exit and 2025 return, and Kalshi's court win. We end with catastrophe bonds as an older, professional version of the same idea. Dated events were checked against news coverage. Not betting or investment advice.

item.title: Cancer's Second Verb: Converting Tumors Instead of Killing Them
item.description: A walk through a knowledge graph built from Brian Roemmele's X post on a KAIST study (Advanced Science, 2024). As the post tells it, researchers built a 'digital twin' of an intestinal cell's gene network, used an algorithm called BENEIN to pick three genes (MYB, HDAC2, FOXA2), and turned colon cancer cells into normal-like cells in cell lines and mice by maturing them rather than killing them. This is early preclinical work with no human data, described secondhand, and nothing here is medical advice. The graph adds context: differentiation therapy has treated the leukemia APL for decades, the idea builds on Waddington, Kauffman and Yamanaka, and hard-to-drug targets, durability (speculative) and the tumor's surroundings could keep it from becoming a therapy.

item.title: How to Research Anything, Part 2: Why It Works
item.description: Part 2 opens with a quick recap of the method, then looks at why it might work and where it falls short. The knowledge graph adds outside theories, all flagged as interpretation: the guide's 'plateau of diminishing returns' mirrors ecology's rule for when a forager should leave a patch, 'useful a year from now?' estimates how fast a field's facts go stale, and a pre-set 'done' is Herbert Simon's satisficing. Then two tensions the guide leaves unaddressed: AI summaries may erode the outsider's fresh eyes, and expert calls aren't independent witnesses. We close with cross-domain synthesis and the author's compounding research playbook.

item.title: How to Research Anything, Part 1: The Method
item.description: Part 1 of a two-parter on Polymath Investor's practitioner guide to independent research. We walk one made-up project through the whole method: scope a small question that passes the 'So what?' test, cap your time, choose sources that will still matter in a year, skim twenty and read three deeply, check key facts against three independent witnesses, keep one-idea notes with their sources, and decide what 'done' means before you start. The guide is one person's untested advice, and its paywalled section is known only from a teaser. Ends with a teaser for Part 2.

item.title: The Slop Superhighway
item.description: Rhys Sullivan argues that agents flooding human channels like GitHub issues isn't the real failure. The failure is that there's no agent-to-agent channel to carry that traffic, so humans end up as 'meat proxies' copy-pasting between AIs. We walk through his first-person Cloudflare bug story (single-sourced), the 2025 issueslop backlash, what exists today (author-side issue triage, MCP, A2A), and what's still missing: identity, payments, and defenses against prompt injection. We close with economics and liability lenses, which the knowledge graph adds as its own speculative extensions rather than claims from the post.

item.title: When Your GTM Brain Lives in Git
item.description: A two-host walkthrough of a knowledge graph built from John Kutay's post "GTM in git," based on his San Francisco talk "Your GTM Belongs in git." The argument: put as much go-to-market work as possible into a git repo that coding agents can reason over, test and scale, with the repo as the "logical brain" and hosted infrastructure taking over only when scale demands it. Covers Rippling's GrowthOS (usage figures are self-reported), agent harnesses and sandboxes, GTM evals, context engineering and shared definitions, and the marketer-as-AI-engineer shift. Also the graph's own additions: a GitOps lineage, a governance caution about agents querying production data, and why "ideas become the bottleneck" is still a contested prediction.

item.title: Super Is Not Superior
item.description: A deep dive into Tejas Kumar's essay "AI Is Now SI: Super Intelligence Isn't Superior," via a knowledge graph of its argument. The essay says "super" describes task performance while "superior" claims worth, and that renaming AI "Super Intelligence" blurs the two. Covers Bostrom's definition of superintelligence, real machine milestones, the BCG "jagged frontier" study, the golden calf, Calvin's "forge of idols," the sun renamed "the greater light" in Genesis, and the essay's case for loyalty as a willingness to overpay. 2026 events are as reported in the essay.

item.title: Fine-Tuning at Home: Beat Frontier Models With 8 Steps
item.description: A two-host walkthrough of a knowledge graph built from Maxime Rivest's article "Even you can now fine-tune an LLM, and maybe you finally should." The claim: with a coding agent, a frontier "teacher" model and LoRA adapters on consumer hardware, fine-tuning a task-specific model is now something one person can do. Covers the eight-step workflow, synthetic distillation, why training loss kept improving while rubric scores plateaued, the roughly 1,000-example saturation point, the break-even math (about 170 papers per hour), licensing limits on training with model outputs, and the last-mile accuracy problem. Benchmark figures are the author's own reported results.
